💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a latest state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models.
  • One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture.
  • According to recent reports, we wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a latest state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here.

One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs (sm100), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ.

According to recent reports, we wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint. Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs, and let it run experiments for an afternoon.

Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.

The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script (bench.py):.

Industry observers note that bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled.

The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure:.

The baseline was our existing org endpoint config: SGLang with --attention-backend fa4 and no speculative decoding.

According to recent reports, single-user decode speed (median of 12 requests). vLLM + DSpark reaches ~95% of the memory-bandwidth ceiling at its measured acceptance rate.

¹ SGLang's RTX PRO 6000 DSpark recipe caps --max-running-requests at 4. Raising it to 8 reached 660 tok/s, still behind vLLM. ² Includes ~160 ms of client-to-endpoint network round trip.

All of the speedup comes from switching to vLLM nightly (+15% over SGLang without speculation, 136 → 157 tok/s), enabling DSpark with 7 drafts and probabilistic draft sampling (+21% on top, 157 → 190.6 tok/s across four runs: 189.3, 190.4, 191.1, and 190.7), and adding two memory flags so vLLM's DSpark setup actually starts on 96 GB:.

Both num_speculative_tokens: 7 and draft_sample_method: "probabilistic" were validated directly: shorter draft counts (such as 5) are rejected at startup because both engines enforce the checkpoint's fixed block size, and switching to greedy draft sampling dropped vLLM decode speed by 11% at temperature 1.0 (see What didn't work).

Before tuning, the agent probed the RTX PRO 6000 inside a Job (1,469 GB/s copy bandwidth, 416 TFLOPS BF16, 792 TFLOPS FP8) and read tensor sizes from the safetensors header. Because every token makes 48 layer visits, plain decode re-reads ~2.7 GB of attention and dense weights, ~2 GB of routed experts (8 of 128 per layer), and ~0.9 GB for the LM head. At 1,469 GB/s, that gives a single-user bandwidth ceiling of ~256 tok/s. Without speculation, vLLM at 157 tok/s hits 61% of that ceiling, mostly limited by kernel launch latency across 48 visits.

Speculative decoding changes the memory math on an MoE. Verifying 8 positions together activates the union of their routed experts, reading roughly 40% of each layer's experts instead of 6%. At our measured acceptance of ~2.3 tokens per step at temperature 1.0 (per-position acceptance drops from 0.6 on the first draft to 0.33 and 0.19), the bandwidth ceiling falls to ~201 tok/s. At 190.6 tok/s, vLLM + DSpark is already at ~95% of hardware bandwidth, so further flag tuning has almost nowhere left to go. Moving past 190 tok/s would take a drafter with higher acceptance at temperature 1.0 or a verification path that touches fewer experts per layer.

Most candidate flags were unsupported, noisy, or slower:.

We also skipped rejection_sample_method: "fly" and "synthetic" on purpose because they alter the output distribution, and we wanted a strictly lossless speedup.

A few measurement issues caught us along the way:.

Before deploying, we pinned the exact vLLM nightly digest (vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:eaa63fd6…, build 0.34.0rc1.dev1235+gf2f9edcac) and ran the acceptance gates inside a Job:.

Once those passed, we deployed the endpoint with a single hf endpoints deploy command, pinning both the image digest and model revision (authenticated access, scale-to-zero after 60 idle minutes):.

Running bench.py against the live endpoint gave 194.9 tok/s single-user, matching the Job runs once network latency is accounted for.

In a recent development, everything from this run (PLAN.md, THEORY.md, jobs/driver.py, submit.sh, deploy.sh, and the raw ledger-*.jsonl files) is in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb. To reuse the loop on another model, put your candidate and control server commands into a configs/plan-*.json file and submit it to whichever HF Jobs GPU flavor matches your target endpoint.

There is Dflash2 for it already.Quite a bit faster.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Greenhouse is still the single largest job board source across mid-market and late-stage tech companies. Out of 81 AI and devtools companies we benchmarked, 31 boards (5,214 open roles) ran on Greenhouse, including anthropic.com (500 tracked roles, median $335,000), stripe.com (500 roles), cloudflare.com (500 roles, median $207,500), databricks.com (500 roles, median $213,750), datadoghq.com (386 roles), and coinbase.com (250 roles, 89.2% remote).

The public JSON endpoint requires no API key and returns an entire company's job board in one GET:.

Industry observers note that that looks trivial on paper. In practice, four small quirks in Greenhouse's JSON payload quietly corrupt downstream data if you do not guard against them.

Sources indicate that if you hit /v1/boards//jobs without ?content=true, Greenhouse still returns 200 OK with every job title, location, and URL, so your scraper looks healthy. The content field is simply omitted. You get zero job descriptions, zero tech-stack keywords, and zero pay transparency ranges. Always append ?content=true when you need anything beyond titles and office counts (and skip it if you only need a fast headcount diff, because responses shrink by 10-20x).

Recent findings suggest that even with ?content=true, the content string is not raw HTML. Greenhouse escapes tags into HTML entities like

We are hiring...

, and on boards where recruiters pasted text from Google Docs or Workday, you occasionally see double-encoded sequences (<p>) plus UTF-8 non-breaking spaces (\xc2\xa0).

If you run a single HTML tag stripper without unescaping first, nothing gets stripped because there are no < characters yet. If you unescape once, double-encoded blocks still leak < into your text.

In Go, we unescape up to twice and then strip tags (dropping.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English.
  • We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness.
  • Industry observers note that A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

Industry observers note that A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:.

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:.

Industry observers note that the key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

It has been revealed that because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Recent findings suggest that search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

Recent findings suggest that the fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:.

Sources indicate that you do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:.

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

Industry observers note that nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Sources indicate that voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

According to recent reports, new to CUGA? Here are some places to start:.

Spaces you can try in your browser:.

More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog:.

This is an interesting example of how voice agents can support Indic languages and make AI more accessible to diverse owners. I think AI agent cost optimization is also worth considering when developing voice-based solutions, as managing compute resources and usage costs can help make these applications more practical to scale. #138087. Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1687 w)

Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished.
  • According to recent reports, these ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science.
  • Industry observers note that to better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

According to recent reports, these ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

Industry observers note that to better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

In a recent development, another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

It has been revealed that for many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing upcoming ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Sources indicate that several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

According to recent reports, these examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

Recent findings suggest that these evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

According to recent reports, an early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”.

It has been revealed that some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

In a recent development, participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher said.

Recent findings suggest that context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

Recent findings suggest that the same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

Recent findings suggest that this is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

Researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

Industry observers note that it will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify important concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

According to recent reports, still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

Domain Verification Polling: Observable Rechecks Across Customer and Platform Zones

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Schedule bounded domain verification retries and expose a manual re-check button in the internal admin console.
  • Industry observers note that TL;DR: Keep verification running after the tab closes.
  • According to recent reports, before: an administrator adds a domain, clicks Verify, and sees “pending.” The onboarding session ends before propagation does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Schedule bounded domain verification retries and expose a manual re-check button in the internal admin console. The deciding constraint is zone ownership: your platform can act on records it owns, but a customer-owned zone requires a clear handoff and an explanation of what the verifier is still waiting to observe.

Industry observers note that TL;DR: Keep verification running after the tab closes. Show the reason for waiting, the last check, and the next scheduled attempt. A manual re-check should refresh the same evidence and share the same attempt budget. For developer tools that connect customer domains to mail, track the DNS-to-email handoff too; a generic green badge cannot explain which prerequisite actually passed.

According to recent reports, before: an administrator adds a domain, clicks Verify, and sees “pending.” The onboarding session ends before propagation does. A one-shot check leaves the administrator guessing about whether to change the record again, wait, or contact support.

After: the console highlights an observed state and the action that follows from it. A proposed message might read: “Required DNS evidence has not been observed. Last checked at 10:04 UTC; next check at 10:09 UTC. Re-check after saving your records.” Those times illustrate UI copy, not a propagation guarantee. If the verifier cannot distinguish an absent record from another cause, say that the required evidence has not been observed; don't invent a diagnosis.

Industry observers note that the diagram in words is small: zone owner saves a record → scheduled or manual trigger requests a check → the worker records evidence → the console explains the next action → the mail workflow consumes its own domain status. Every arrow needs an owner. For a customer-owned zone, the console should explain what the customer must publish. For a platform-owned zone, it should direct the record change to the platform's record-management workflow. In either case, submitting a change and observing the required DNS evidence belong to separate steps.

In a recent development, that distinction matters after a DKIM rotation as well as during initial onboarding. The records and the mail service that depends on them need a renewed handoff. Saving yesterday's successful onboarding badge does not establish that today's required record has been observed.

According to recent reports, use a durable job record so scheduled work survives the browser session. As an illustrative application policy, allow 6 automatic attempts, with delays of 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 minutes between attempts. These are design choices to review against your onboarding needs; they are neither vendor defaults nor promises about DNS propagation. After the final attempt, retain the evidence and expose an explicit action to start a new bounded verification run.

According to recent reports, A manual re-check should be useful immediately without creating unlimited parallel work. Have it enter the same worker path, coalesce requests while a check is active, and consume an attempt from the current budget. Tell the customer when a check is already running or the budget has ended. Otherwise, the button promises control while silently producing more background jobs.

Sources indicate that for an application-owned event, record the domain, zone owner, verification-run identifier, trigger type, attempt number, observation time, and outcome reason. Those are proposed fields for your own event model, not vendor response fields. Separate “check could not complete” from “check completed without the required evidence.” A transport problem should not turn into instructions to edit a customer's DNS. Likewise, do not treat a successful HTTP response as proof that the domain is verified: transport success and verification success answer different questions.

Recent findings suggest that the useful metrics follow directly. Count exhausted runs by zone ownership and reason; measure elapsed time to observed completion; watch manual re-checks per run. A burst of manual checks can point to confusing copy or an interval that feels too long. It does not, by itself, establish a DNS-provider problem. Alert on checks that stop executing, and surface exhausted customer runs as actionable onboarding work. Pending domains alone make a noisy alert.

Keep three real alternatives on the shortlist: Amazon Route 53, Cloudflare DNS, and Google Cloud DNS. Compare the account boundary before comparing convenience. The mail side still needs its own choice.

According to recent reports, these are deployment choices to evaluate, not claims that the services impose identical verification schedules. Their primary documentation is linked below. Existing account ownership can make any of these sensible, and none of the pairings removes the need to explain a pending check.

In a recent development, infrai combines DNS and email under one API key and one bill, with a plain REST API and no SDK to install. It is a strong option when the verification worker and mail-domain lookup should share credentials: an HTTP client can call both, and unified billing keeps the workflow on one invoice. The trade-off is one vendor to trust and one outage surface. If your organization requires separate providers or already delegates its zones through AWS accounts, Route 53 with SES may fit better than consolidating the integration.

The alternative glue is concrete. With Route 53 plus SES, you connect two service workflows within AWS; counting them as two independent vendor signups would be misleading. With Cloudflare plus Resend, you connect two provider accounts when you operate both. In either arrangement, your application must retain domain identity, map observed DNS evidence to mail-domain status, schedule another check when appropriate, and explain a rotated record that has not yet been observed. That is where SPF/DKIM onboarding becomes an ongoing workflow rather than a copy-paste between dashboards.

Here is a small TypeScript identity handoff using two read routes. It checks identity rather than declaring verification success. Configure INFRAI_BASE_URL with the documented HTTPS API base ending in /v1, INFRAI_API_KEY with the server-side key, and DOMAIN with the domain being onboarded. Supply DNS_DOMAIN_GET_QUERY as a URL query string containing the lookup parameters declared by the request schema. Parameter names are not assumed here.

The same base URL and bearer key serve both requests. The first response must contain the exact requested domain as a string value before that observed value enters the mail-domain lookup. A response representing identity differently fails closed and requires a schema-specific adapter. No response field named “verified” is guessed. Run the example in a server-side TypeScript environment with fetch support.

The reads are safe to repeat. The example bounds HTTP attempts at 3 and honors Retry-After on rate limits. That small HTTP retry budget is separate from the durable verification schedule. For production logs, extract approved status fields instead of retaining these entire response bodies.

Industry observers note that this snippet establishes the seam. A production worker still needs schema-specific interpretation of both responses before marking DNS evidence or mail readiness complete. Its scheduled and manual verification triggers should invoke the documented verification operation with the required request shape and an idempotency policy; a read alone does not initiate that operation. Keeping those responsibilities explicit prevents an identity lookup from masquerading as an onboarding check.

A button only helps while someone is looking at it. DNS propagation can outlast the onboarding session, so bounded scheduled retries let the customer close the tab and return to a completed state. The manual action serves a different moment: the customer has just published a record and wants fresh evidence without waiting for your interval. Both triggers earn their place.

The other likely objection is that owning the zone should eliminate the wait. It changes who can make the record change and who gets the next action. It does not make “change submitted,” “required evidence observed,” and “mail domain ready” interchangeable statements. Preserve those distinctions in the event trail and in the console copy.

Then keep the final state useful: after the budget ends, show the last observation, why the run stopped, and who can act next. A stopped polling job is an application policy outcome. Give the administrator enough evidence to decide what to do with it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate.

It has been revealed that this is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

In a recent development, multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we upgrade when we're dealing with many agents?

It has been revealed that in this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

According to recent reports, we've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI revealed that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

Industry observers note that but swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

A significant swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

Recent findings suggest that start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

Sources indicate that four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

We understand that question through this simple expectation.

It has been revealed that we'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

According to recent reports, this creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

Recent findings suggest that A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

In a recent development, agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:.

A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

Sources indicate that A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:.

The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

It has been revealed that the main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

According to recent reports, in this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:.

For illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

For every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

In TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

According to recent reports, our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per update (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

According to recent reports, over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

Industry observers note that the team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

Industry observers note that the team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:.

That is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

Notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

No agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each upgrade collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:.

With eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

In a recent development, the model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each enhancement generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts rapidly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:.

The figures above describe our original 75-update experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

In a recent development, sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

Sources indicate that the command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

One TRL rollout contains a whole team conversation. The trainer compares eight attempts at the same problem and gives all four agents in an attempt the same advantage. Each revision uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

It has been revealed that this shorter run is cheaper than our original experiment, and it stops earlier on the learning curve. TRL's run of this example took about 4.8 hours on two H100s and reached 60.9% held-out success at checkpoint 50.

To run closer to our original experiment, change the training flags to --updates 75 --teams-per-revision 256 --concurrent-teams 256, replace checkpoint-50 with checkpoint-75 in the script, and raise the job's --timeout to 24h. That is three times as many rollouts. The two codebases still differ in details such as the system prompt, so expect similar results rather than an exact replication.

It has been revealed that once the job completes, sync the bucket to a local folder. It holds the two evaluation files, the Trackio data, the TRL revision and the checkpoint-50 weights, which are the largest download. In the dashboard, compare team/success, team/messages and team/tokens over training. The job logs also give the held-out success rate for the base model and checkpoint 50. Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

Industry observers note that this first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also indicates why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I want to share my open-source Flutter MCP Suite — a set of 5 Dart and Flutter packages for building AI agents with Model Context Protocol (MCP), generative UI (A2UI), and local on-device models.

In a recent development, to be honest, I did not write all this code by hand. I designed the structure, guided the work, and maintain the packages using AI coding agents — mainly Antigravity, and now also my own open-source tool TealKit Coder, which is built on top of dart_mcp_core.

Using the packages every day inside a real coding agent helped find many real bugs quickly — like context compression loops, local model template errors, and Android file-saving complications — so we could fix them and add tests right away.

In a recent development, the base package is dart_mcp_core. It is pure Dart with no Flutter dependencies (160/160 pub.dev points, 99+ unit tests).

Because it does not depend on Flutter, the same agent engine works everywhere:.

With flutter_a2ui_mcp (using a2ui_flutter ^0.5.0 and a2ui_core ^0.9.0), the AI can show interactive Flutter widgets directly inside the chat instead of only plain text.

In v1.2.1, it uses A2UI 1.0 Express by default:.

Express uses about half as many tokens as raw JSON, checks the output against your widget catalog, and still falls back to normal JSON if a smaller model outputs JSON instead.

In a recent development, if you want to run models offline on Android, iOS, or Desktop, flutter_ui_mcp_embedded connects llamadart (^0.21.0) to dart_mcp_core. It supports both GGUF (llama.cpp) and LiteRT-LM (.litertlm) models, and includes a HuggingFace model search dialog.

If you try it out or have any feedback, feel free to leave a comment or open an matter on GitHub!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From repetitive manual tasks to a tested and customizable open-source CLI.

It has been revealed that automation is one of the fundamental principles of DevOps and software engineering. However, even developers who automate complex infrastructure and deployment workflows often perform repetitive tasks when starting a latest software project.

Recent findings suggest that creating directories, initializing Git repositories, configuring remote repositories, and opening development environments are simple operations. When repeated frequently, however, they become unnecessary friction in the development workflow.

This observation motivated me to develop Init Flow, an open-source command-line interface written in Bash to automate and standardize project initialization.

The project combines Linux automation, Git, GitHub CLI, software engineering practices, and continuous integration into a lightweight development tool.

In this article, I will introduce Init Flow, demonstrate its capabilities, explain its architectural decisions, and share lessons learned while developing and releasing version v0.2.0.

A typical project initialization workflow might involve several manual commands:.

Although each command is relatively simple, this workflow assumes that:.

Without proper validation and error handling, these assumptions can lead to inconsistent environments, unexpected failures, or conflicts with existing projects.

The challenge was not simply to combine commands into a shell script, but to create a reliable, predictable, and maintainable CLI.

Init Flow automates project initialization through a single command:.

The goal is to reduce repetitive work while maintaining control over the initialization process.

Init Flow is distributed under the MIT License and is presently focused on Linux environments.

For the default workflow, you need:.

Authenticate with GitHub CLI if necessary:.

Clone the published version of the repository:.

The installer creates a symbolic link in:.

No root privileges are required.

Make sure this directory is available in your PATH.

This initializes a local project, creates a public GitHub repository, and opens Visual Studio Code.

The uninstaller removes only the symbolic link associated with the expected installation.

The first release focused on establishing a functional project initialization workflow.

Version v0.2.0 — Configuration and Customization extends that foundation with seven command-line options.

These options make Init Flow adaptable to different development workflows.

It has been revealed that the README is generated locally. Init Flow does not automatically commit or push it.

This workflow requires Git but does not require GitHub CLI authentication or Visual Studio Code.

Dry-run mode displays the planned operation without creating directories, initializing Git repositories, creating remote repositories, or opening the editor.

Remote repository availability is not verified during a dry run.

One of the main architectural goals was to keep the implementation simple without sacrificing reliability.

Rather than introducing external frameworks or additional runtime dependencies, Init Flow uses Bash and existing development tools.

The repository is organized around clear responsibilities:.

The main executable handles command execution, while installation, uninstallation, testing, and documentation remain separated.

Version v0.2.0 introduces centralized argument parsing.

Arguments are validated before operations that modify the filesystem or interact with GitHub.

For example, combining --local with --private is rejected because repository visibility has no meaning when no remote repository is created.

Not every execution mode requires the same dependencies.

Checking dependencies according to the selected execution mode avoids imposing unnecessary requirements on users.

Init Flow resolves the base project directory using the following precedence:.

This allows customers to customize their development environment without modifying the source code.

Relative paths and paths containing spaces are also supported.

Shell automation can become dangerous when user input is passed directly to system commands without validation.

For this reason, Init Flow prioritizes defensive programming.

The implementation uses Bash strict mode:.

However, strict mode alone is not sufficient. Reliable shell scripts also require explicit validation and appropriate error handling.

The project follows several defensive principles:.

Dry-run mode adds another layer of operational safety by allowing users to inspect planned actions before execution.

It has been revealed that repository visibility remains public by default for backward compatibility. Users working with private projects should explicitly select --private or use --local.

A major goal of Init Flow is to demonstrate that even relatively small shell-based tools benefit from structured software engineering practices.

The project evolved from 30 automated tests in v0.1.0 to 58 automated tests in v0.2.0.

The test suites cover four main areas:.

Integration tests use mocks to simulate external commands such as Git, GitHub CLI, and Visual Studio Code where appropriate.

This prevents automated tests from accidentally creating real GitHub repositories or interacting with external services.

ShellCheck is used to identify common shell scripting problems, including quoting issues, unsafe expansions, and other potentially unreliable patterns.

Each script is checked individually:.

GitHub Actions automates the validation process, including:.

The release workflow requires successful CI validation before publishing a new version.

The published tag is also validated through an isolated post-release smoke test, ensuring that the distributed version behaves as expected.

One of the most valuable lessons during the v0.2.0 release came from an unexpected CI failure.

All local tests had passed, but the integration tests failed in GitHub Actions.

The root cause was a dependency on ripgrep (rg) that was available in my local development environment but absent from the CI runner.

The affected test used a command similar to:.

The solution was to replace it with a standard tool already available in the target environment:.

Industry observers note that another test used a pipeline to verify dry-run output. Early termination by the search command could produce a broken pipe.

Instead of relying on that pipeline, the output was captured and evaluated directly:.

The correction preserved the original assertions while removing the unnecessary dependency and the problematic pipeline.

After the fix, the affected integration suite passed all 30 tests, and GitHub Actions successfully validated the release candidate.

This experience reinforced several engineering principles:.

The fix was recorded in a dedicated Conventional Commit:.

These are potential directions rather than committed features for the next release.

The long-term objective is to reach a stable v1.0.0 while preserving simplicity, reliability, and maintainability.

Developing Init Flow has been an opportunity to apply software engineering and DevOps principles to a practical automation problem.

The project demonstrates how a Bash CLI can evolve beyond a collection of shell commands into a structured, tested, documented, and versioned open-source tool.

Its development reinforces the importance of:.

Version v0.2.0 represents another step toward a reliable and extensible project initialization tool.

If you work with Linux, Bash, DevOps, or developer automation, feel free to explore the repository, experiment with the CLI, report concerns, or suggest improvements.

Latest Update: Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (392 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face.
  • Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve.
  • It has been revealed that you can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

It has been revealed that you can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

The dashboard demonstrates two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:.

Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

Recent findings suggest that we benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

Recent findings suggest that the model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Industry observers note that standard results use ///.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename.

#138069. Phaser 3: Invalid Texture Atlas JSON Hash given, missing 'frames' Object

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (521 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Phaser 3: Invalid Texture Atlas JSON Hash given, missing 'frames' Object

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While the atlas loads, the Console prints Invalid Texture Atlas JSON Hash given, missing 'frames' Object.
  • Phaser's Hash atlas parser expects a JSON object whose top level contains a frames object keyed by frame name.
  • It has been revealed that A re-export from the packing tool is the most common time for this to surface, because the exporter's format option can change between projects, and an old loader config kept from the previous atlas then points at the new structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While the atlas loads, the Console prints Invalid Texture Atlas JSON Hash given, missing 'frames' Object. The texture registers with only its base frame, and any lookup by frame name comes back empty or falls back to the first frame. Animations built from the atlas run with missing frames, sprites show the wrong tile, and the missing-frame warning follows once the animation tries to resolve names that were never parsed.

Phaser's Hash atlas parser expects a JSON object whose top level contains a frames object keyed by frame name. The parser checks for that key first; when it is absent, it aborts the parse and keeps only the __BASE frame, so every named frame later in the file is ignored. The missing key usually means one of four mismatches. The atlas was exported in Array format, a JSON whose top level holds a frames array of records, but the code feeds it through the Hash loader, or the reverse. The JSON was truncated, hand-edited, or saved as text so its structure no longer parses as the expected object. The request returned an HTML error page or a redirect body instead of the JSON file, and the parser tried to read that markup as atlas data. Or the JSON and the image were paired under mismatched keys, so the atlas that loads does not match the texture the animation references.

It has been revealed that A re-export from the packing tool is the most common time for this to surface, because the exporter's format option can change between projects, and an old loader config kept from the previous atlas then points at the new structure. The JSON can also look almost correct at a glance: a frames entry may exist one level deeper, or the file may use the Array records while the code expects name keys.

Recent findings suggest that open the atlas JSON in a text editor and read its top-level keys. A Hash atlas exposes an object under frames, with entries keyed by frame name; an Array atlas exposes frames as a list of records that each carry a filename field. Check the browser Network panel for the JSON request and confirm the response status is 200 and the body is JSON rather than an HTML error page. Also confirm the loader call passes both the image and the JSON under matching keys.

After it loads, print the frame names the texture actually holds:.

In a recent development, A healthy Hash atlas lists named frames such as walk_1, walk_2. A broken one lists only the base frame, or an empty list, which confirms the parser stopped before reading the frames object.

Match the exporter format to the loader you call, and repair the JSON before pairing it with the image:.

After the change, verify in code rather than by watching the canvas: log frameTotal and check that each expected frame name returns true from has, and confirm the parser warning no longer appears in the Console on load.

The exact engine message and source location for this atlas warning are documented in the error reference.

BlazorJS or SpawnJS? Which to use, and how to move

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpawnDev has two libraries that let C# use browser APIs: SpawnDev.BlazorJS and SpawnDev.SpawnJS.
  • Sources indicate that the short answer: start latest projects on SpawnJS.
  • In a recent development, spawnDev.BlazorJS was first published in December 2022 and has over 222,000 NuGet downloads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpawnDev has two libraries that let C# use browser APIs: SpawnDev.BlazorJS and SpawnDev.SpawnJS. If you are starting a project, or you already use one, you will want to know which to pick and what moving costs.

Sources indicate that the short answer: start latest projects on SpawnJS. If your app runs well on BlazorJS, there is no rush; it is still supported. When you do move, most of your code stays the same.

In a recent development, spawnDev.BlazorJS was first published in December 2022 and has over 222,000 NuGet downloads. It works through Blazor's own JavaScript interop.

SpawnDev.SpawnJS is the newer library. It talks to JavaScript through .NET's JSImport and JSExport and does not need Blazor at all.

The SpawnJS README reports a test app that went from about 30 MB to about 9 MB when trimmed. In the small example below, the published apps were 19.5 MB on SpawnJS and 22.5 MB on BlazorJS, counting the compressed copies of each file.

Because SpawnJS does not depend on Blazor, the same C# can run where Blazor never does: a plain .NET WebAssembly app, a Web Worker, a browser extension, or a .NET WebAssembly console app running under Node.js with no browser at all.

Recent findings suggest that that last one is not a curiosity. SpawnDev.ILGPU, our GPU library, runs its shared GPU test suite that way: a .NET WebAssembly console app under Node.js, using SpawnJS for every JavaScript call, with real WebGPU from the webgpu npm package, the Dawn project's own binding. On an RTX 4070, all 876 tests that apply there pass. The other 22 are skipped: 17 belong to other backends, and 5 check for a feature Node does not have, such as a canvas or a video frame, and say so.

The first run found something a browser-only test run never could: under Node, the library never loaded one of its WebGPU helper scripts, so dispatch batching quietly switched off. That is fixed in SpawnDev.ILGPU 5.4.52.

In a recent development, to try it yourself, Example 08 runs a GPU kernel from C# under Node and prints the GPU it found. It needs Node 22 or later and the .NET wasm-tools workload.

BlazorJS is built on Blazor's own interop, so it needs a Blazor app.

Article 1 built a recipe page that keeps the screen awake and copies to the clipboard with SpawnJS. We wrote the same page with BlazorJS, and the same browser tests pass for both.

The page itself did not change except for one line, the runtime you inject:.

Everything else, Navigator, WakeLock, Clipboard, the += and -= events, using, is the same in both libraries.

2. Change the start-up lines in Program.cs.

Industry observers note that 3. Change the namespaces in _Imports.razor and your C# files: SpawnDev.BlazorJS becomes SpawnDev.SpawnJS, and SpawnDev.BlazorJS.JSObjects becomes SpawnDev.SpawnJS.JSObjects.

According to recent reports, 4. Change the injected runtime: BlazorJSRuntime becomes SpawnJSRuntime.

That was the whole move for our example.

Your own wrappers. If you wrote classes for a JavaScript library, the base class and the reference type change: JSObject becomes SpawnJSObject, and the constructor takes a SpawnJSObjectReference instead of an IJSInProcessObjectReference. Both libraries' own Audio wrapper highlights it:.

Industry observers note that calls by name. BlazorJS takes the arguments as objects and names only the return type. SpawnJS names every argument type, then the return type:.

The compiler points at each of these, so the move is a list of build errors to work through, not a hunt.

Matching packages. Several libraries come in both families, such as SpawnDev.BlazorJS.WebWorkers and SpawnDev.SpawnJS.WebWorkers, and SpawnDev.BlazorJS.Cryptography and SpawnDev.SpawnJS.Cryptography. Move each to its SpawnJS twin at the same time.

Both versions of the page are in the example repo:.

The SpawnJS version is in BrowserApis, next to it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A classic grilled cheese is a thing of both beauty and comfort. And of course, a simple sandwich such as this is open to interpretation, with many putting their own spin on it, like making it Swiss-style with raclette cheese or switching up the grilling process by using an air fryer, like Ree Drummond. But there's an easy addition you can make to your next grilled cheese that will make it even tastier (and it's not mayo or butter, though you can certainly use either): It's store-bought caramelized onion dip.

Sources indicate that when spread onto the bread and covered in cheese, then warmed through in a hot pan, caramelized onion dip brings a burst of flavor and a compelling texture to the sandwich. Of course, it's definitely savory, but the caramelized onions also introduce a subtly sweet element to grilled cheese, creating a flavor sensation that is much more interesting for your taste buds. Meanwhile, the dip melts into the cheese, adding to the creaminess, while the onions introduce a little toothsome variety to chew on, beyond the softness of the filling and the crispness of the bread.

Recent findings suggest that trader Joe's Caramelized Onion Dip is one great store-bought option, and it's part of the store's regular lineup, so you should be able to find it year-round (unless it has sold out). Whole Foods also sells a version under its 365 brand, which Amazon Prime members can shop for on Amazon.

If you have the desire to take things a step further, you might try a mix-in or two that can elevate the taste of the dip (and therefore, your entire sandwich). That might include some dried cranberries, which can help draw out the aforementioned sweetness of the onions, creating an even bolder contrast in your salty grilled cheese. You also might play to the richness and crumble up some crisp bacon into the base. Or enhance the savory, aromatic vibes by adding both thinly sliced scallions and chives.

Now, if you're having trouble finding caramelized onion dip at your grocery store, you could always make your own, though cooking down the onions properly can be laborious. If standing over your stove for 45 minutes doesn't appeal to you, Ina Garten cuts down on the time by using a larger pot, which allows the onions to cook more evenly and efficiently. But if you'd rather skip the cooking altogether, you might find the adjacent caramelized onion jam on store shelves. This won't be as creamy as the dip, but it will still impart that same rich, savory, and slightly sweet flavor, so it's a decent substitution.
